title: Section 34 Arbitration Act — Set aside the award

content.overview: Section 34 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 is the exclusive court recourse against an arbitral award. It is an application to set aside, not an appeal on facts or evidence. The grounds include party incapacity, an invalid arbitration agreement, want of proper notice or inability to present the case, a decision beyond the scope of the submission, a tribunal constituted or a procedure conducted otherwise than as agreed or as the Act provides, non-arbitrability, and conflict with the public policy of India. For a domestic award other than an award arising out of an international commercial arbitration, patent illegality appearing on the face of the award is an additional ground under s. 34(2A), with an express bar on setting aside merely for erroneous application of the law or reappreciation of evidence. The application must be made within three months of receipt of the award, or of disposal of a request under s. 33, and the court may entertain it within a further thirty days on sufficient cause, but not thereafter.
content.study: Keep the existing point that three months plus thirty days is the outer limit and that public policy is not a second hearing. Add the ground map and the domestic patent-illegality limit. Stay is not automatic; that is s. 36.

learningObjectives: State that s. 34 is the only recourse against the award and is not an appeal.
List the s. 34(2) and s. 34(2A) grounds without treating patent illegality as a rehearing.

enhancement.definition: Section 34 provides the sole court application to set aside an arbitral award on enumerated grounds, within three months of receipt plus a further thirty days on sufficient cause and no more.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The court does not sit in appeal over the award. Interference is confined to the statutory grounds. Patent illegality on the face of a qualifying domestic award is not a licence to reappreciate evidence.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, s. 34, including s. 34(2), s. 34(2A) and s. 34(3); public-policy explanation in s. 34; correction and interpretation window in s. 33 feeds the limitation start; stay and enforcement are s. 36.
essentialIngredients: Arbitral award received, or s. 33 request disposed of
Ground under s. 34(2) or, for a qualifying domestic award, patent illegality on the face under s. 34(2A)
Public policy confined to the statutory explanation, not a merits review
Three months, extendable by thirty days on sufficient cause, not thereafter
enhancement.detailedExplanation: The opening of s. 34 is exclusive: recourse to a court against an arbitral award may be made only by an application for setting aside. Party-proved grounds cover incapacity, invalidity of the agreement, notice and opportunity, excess of scope, and improper composition or procedure. Court-examined grounds cover non-arbitrable subject matter and conflict with the public policy of India. The explanation of public policy covers induced or affected by fraud or corruption, contravention of the fundamental policy of Indian law, and conflict with the most basic notions of morality or justice. Section 34(2A) adds patent illegality on the face of the award for domestic awards other than international commercial arbitration awards, and it says that an award shall not be set aside merely on the ground of an erroneous application of the law or by reappreciation of evidence. Section 34(3) is a hard limitation: three months from receipt, a further thirty days if sufficient cause is shown, and not thereafter. Filing under s. 34 does not itself stay the award; s. 36 is the enforcement and stay provision.
examples: The award decides a claim never submitted to arbitration; excess of scope is the s. 34 ground.
A domestic non-ICA award shows patent illegality on its face; s. 34(2A) is examined, but the court does not reappreciate evidence.
The application is filed after three months plus thirty days from receipt; s. 34(3) bars it.
The award-debtor files s. 34 and assumes execution is stayed; that assumption is wrong and belongs to s. 36.
enhancement.problemApplication: Fix the receipt date and the s. 33 disposal date if any; test the outer limit; classify the award as domestic or international commercial before using s. 34(2A); plead a statutory ground; keep merits review out; send stay to s. 36.

keyTakeaways: Section 34 is the only court recourse and is not an appeal.
Patent illegality does not apply to an international commercial arbitration award and is not a rehearing.
The further thirty days cannot be extended.
